item.title: The Upgrade of Managed IT Services: A New Option for SMB IT in the AI Era
item.description:
This post doesn’t claim to settle anything. It lays out a question I’ve been turning over for two years: is the way SMBs buy IT about to change? My leaning is yes. This article looks at it mainly through the lens of technology development, with a quick pass at the money. Push back if I’ve got it wrong.

1. Why SMB IT Supply Is Broken

Most SMBs assemble IT like this: find someone to fix computers, hire an outsourcing firm to build business systems, and once the project ships, nobody owns it. The outsourcing problem is requirements translation — the business says “I want to know at any moment which orders might be late,” and by the time it lands in the contract it has become a few screens plus a list of feature points. Acceptance passes; the business problem may still be unsolved. Traditional MSPs only cover computers, networks, and backups — they can’t afford to keep people who understand the business, can plan, and will take responsibility. The result is a gap in the middle: someone manages the cables, nobody manages the systems, and nobody at all manages “where the money goes over the next three years.”

item.title: Enterprise AI Adoption: Organizational Context, Internal FDEs, and Scenario Gates
item.description:
This post distills the framework we developed while building enterprise AI adoption plans: a four-level evolution path, four types of enterprise context, internal FDEs, three scenario gates, a five-stage rollout, and four governance pillars. Most AI projects stall at the pilot stage because nobody owns the organization, the data, and the processes—not because of the technology.

Over the past two years, companies have bought AI in nearly identical ways: purchase a batch of seats, run a few training sessions, pick two departments to pilot, then wait for the reports. Six months later, most of them are stuck at “individuals know how to use it,” while organizational capability hasn’t moved an inch.

item.title: AI-Native Engineering: Artifact Chains, Gates, and Metrics
item.description:
This is what we learned after getting an AI-native development process running end to end: the artifact chain, the distinction between constraints and assumptions, three-valued gates, three-layer metrics, and four failure modes you will inevitably hit. Installing the tools is year one; hardening the process is the actual transformation.

Last year we rolled AI coding tools into our development team. Three months later we did a delivery review, and the numbers were ugly: plenty of tool usage, no faster delivery. The cause was not the models — it was that we treated them as “faster typewriters” while the process itself never moved an inch.

item.title: API Access and Integrity Risk Catalog
item.description:
This post distills the API governance methodology developed for the OMAPS (麦扑科技) location management system: a risk catalog of 17 control measures for enterprise internal systems, designed for architecture reviews, security requirement writing, and threat modeling.

Scope: enterprise internal systems — systems where the data is a company-level asset and every user is both a user and a maintainer of that asset. This includes CQRS command channels / multi-tenant middle platforms / open APIs (MCP, mini-program mobile clients). Purpose: a standard risk catalog for architecture reviews, security requirements, and threat modeling. Positioning: belongs to the “API Access and Integrity Risk” category, alongside Transport Security and Authentication Security.

item.title: About
item.description:
OMAPS Tech

OMAPS Tech focuses on digital management of outdoor advertising placements. Our core product, OMAPS, unifies placement (ad space) inventory, customer orders, contracts, and financial documents in a single multi-tenant platform.

Website: www.omaps.cn

This Blog

Three kinds of content live here:

  • Architecture & Security: multi-tenant isolation, permission models, API governance, threat modeling, and audit standards;
  • Engineering Practices: hands-on details of the CQRS write channel, review frameworks, state machines, and concurrency control;
  • Codified Standards: conventions written down after the team hit the same pitfalls repeatedly, published so the definitions don’t drift.

Posts come from internal team documents, published after sanitization: no client data, credentials, or production addresses.
